items.rationale: The difference is who owns the control flow: in a workflow your code fixes the steps and their order, in an agent the model decides the next step. Workflows can contain model calls (a), and both can use tools (c); accuracy and cost (d) vary by case and are not the dividing line.

The code fixes the steps and their order; the model only fills in one step (picking a slot), so the code owns the control flow and this is a workflow. A model call inside a flow does not make the model the owner.
In a fixed workflow the code owns the control flow, so every request follows the same path, whatever it asks. That is the cost of a workflow: it cannot adapt to a request its path was not built for.
The agent uses 5 - 2 = 3 more calls per request, and 3 x 300 = 900. Fewer, predictable calls is why a fixed workflow is cheaper when the steps are known.

Finding why prints fail has no known sequence of steps: what to check next depends on what the last result showed, so the model should choose. The other three have steps you can write down in advance, so a fixed workflow fits.

items.answer: The steps are always the same, so code can run them in order with fewer model calls, which is cheaper, faster and more predictable.
accepted: The steps are known in advance, so a workflow is cheaper and more reliable than letting the model decide.
It never varies, so a fixed workflow costs less and behaves more predictably.
The order is always the same, so there is nothing for the model to decide and an agent would only add cost and risk.
items.rationale: Full credit names that the steps are known and fixed, plus at least one benefit: lower cost, speed, or predictability. Saying only that agents are worse, with no reason, is partial.
